title: Service path slowmode investigation walkthrough
content:
Summary:

This is a working walkthrough of the ‘slowmode’ symptom observed on 2025-02-10->2025-02-14: intermittent p99 regressions (250–600ms extra) on the hosted inference path for short prompts (~<64 tokens). Goal is to capture sampling methodology, per-stage decomposition, hypothesis space, experiments run so far, and concrete follow-ups.

Quick TL;DR observations: 
- Bulk of p50/p95 stable; p99 tail spikes are intermittent and correlate with small bursts of concurrent short requests (microbursts) and rare KV cache miss hot-paths.
- Per-stage breakdown shows queuing inside the async-batcher and a trimmed but visible kernel scheduling jitter on GPU node at tail.
- Repro plan: synthetic microburst generator + KV-populate warmup reduces tail by ~30% in canary.

Data collected and timeframe:
- Sample window: 2025-02-10 00:00 -> 2025-02-14 23:59 (production traces + debug sampling).
- Trace count used: 24,386 E2E traces where request latency > 300ms (filtered by route=chat-short and model=redwood-3b-quant).
- Additional controlled replay traces: 5k synthetic runs across 3 seqlen cohorts.
- Traces include per-stage timestamps for: ingress, auth, tokenizer, model-queue-enter, async-batcher-wait, model-run-start, model-run-end, kv-cache-check, egress-serialize, egress-write.

Sampling methodology and cohorts:
- Cohorts: short (<64 tokens), medium (64-512), long (>512). Focus is short cohort (majority of spikes).
- Split by warm vs cold connection (warm = node KV-cache hit & active session within 60s).
- Collected micro-metrics: queue depth, batch size seen by model-run, kv-cache hit boolean, GPU utilization at model-run, kernel-switch counts (from perf counter).

Aggregate numbers (production traces, short cohort):
- p50: 74ms
- p95: 118ms
- p99: 432ms (note high variance, see notes)
- Mean: 95ms
- Tail shape: heavy right skew driven by rare 600–1,200ms outliers that occur ~0.4% of requests in this cohort.

Per-stage breakdown (short cohort, p50/p95/p99):
- ingress: p50 4ms | p95 6ms | p99 12ms
- tokenizer: p50 6ms | p95 9ms | p99 18ms
- model-queue-enter -> async-batcher-wait: p50 18ms | p95 42ms | p99 260ms  <-- major variance source
- async-batcher-hand-off -> model-run-start: p50 3ms | p95 6ms | p99 20ms
- model-run (kernel exec): p50 28ms | p95 44ms | p99 72ms  <-- small but present kernel jitter at tail
- kv-cache-check (when miss): p50 0ms | p95 2ms | p99 88ms  <-- rare kv-miss connected to disk/HBM refill path
- egress-serialize + write: p50 8ms | p95 12ms | p99 18ms
- remainder / unknown instrumentation gap: p99 extra ~44ms in a subset of traces (investigate trace completeness)

Key observations and evidence snippets:
1) Async-batcher queuing amplifies microbursts
   - On traces with p99 latency, batch sizes observed before model-run are often 1 or 2 but queue wait is long (150–400ms).
   - Heap of concurrent short requests arrive within a 40–120ms window and are separated into sequential microbatches due to batching timer and inter-arrival jitter.
   - Hypothesis: batching timer calibration + batching threshold misalignment on short routes.

2) KV-cache miss & refill path
   - ~3% of p99 traces show kv-cache-check cost > 60ms. We correlate these with recent node restarts and occasional eviction storms.
   - Refill path touches HBM->DRAM fallback code path which is noticeably slower and synchronous in implementation.

3) GPU kernel scheduling jitter
   - Perf counters show occasional kernel context switches and 1–2ms scheduling jitter per kernel. Aggregated across tokens/kernels this becomes visible for tail.
   - Higher probability when GPU utilization is 85%+ and co-located background reclaimer runs.

4) Trace instrumentation gaps
   - ~8% of traces had missing timestamps for async-batcher-hand-off. This introduces a small unknown bucket. Need instrumentation fix.

Experiments executed (results):
- Canary A: Reduce batching timer for short route from 20ms -> 6ms. Result: p99 reduced from 432ms -> 312ms (improved tail but increased p95 by ~6ms due to more frequent smaller batches).
- Canary B: Pre-warm KV-cache for selected canary nodes using TTL refresh script before traffic shift. Result: p99 reduced to 298ms for affected nodes; kv-miss occurrences dropped by ~70% across canary.
- Canary C: Isolate GPU node background cron (reclaimer) off noisy nodes. Result: per-kernel jitter reduced slightly; p99 improvement marginal (~4%).

Hypotheses prioritized (ordered):
1) Primary: Batching timer and microburst interaction is dominant tail source for short routes.
2) Secondary: KV-cache miss/refill path causes high single-trace penalties that compound tail distribution.
3) Tertiary: Kernel scheduling under high utilization contributes but is lower impact than 1 and 2.

Actionable next steps / playbook items: 
- Short-term (1–2 days):
  * Roll batching timer change to 30% of short-route traffic (owner: Miguel; ticket: JIRA-1724). Monitor cost impact and p95 tradeoff.
  * Deploy KV TTL refresh warmup to all dedicated nodes serving short cohort and bake for 24h (owner: Lina; ticket: JIRA-1725).
  * Add synthetic microburst harness to staging that replays production arrival patterns (owner: Asha; PR linked above).

- Medium-term (1–3 weeks):
  * Rework kv-cache refill path to be async and non-blocking for request path (owner: eng-storage; ticket: JIRA-1740).
  * Add dynamic batching policy that detects microburst arrival and temporarily reduces timer/thresholds per route instead of platform-wide change (research spike: Evan).
  * Improve trace instrumentation to capture async-batcher-hand-off and kernel scheduling markers (owner: observability; ticket: JIRA-1732).

- Long-term (>1 month):
  * Consider a per-route admission controller that can smooth microbursts by slight rate-limit-backoff + scheduled batching (product evaluation).
  * Explore HBM-resident hot-set promotion and non-blocking refill using background prefetcher.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why do kv-cache eviction storms occur on some nodes after low-util maintenance windows? (link to infra restart logs needed)
- How does per-tenant burstiness interact with global batching policy under multi-tenant GPU pools?
- Cost tradeoff analysis: more aggressive timer reduction increases CPU pressure and increases overall token cost; we need a modeling pass for business impact.

Notes to self and observations from adhoc debugging sessions:
- Repro in staging is flaky; exact inter-arrival jitter pattern matters (saw difference when using Poisson vs recorded arrival times).
- When a batch has one long-tail request (kv-miss), subsequent requests in the same batch don't necessarily get impacted (we hand off earlier). The worst is when requests are serialized across microbatches.
- Slack thread contains a short flamegraph export and example trace ids: trace-20250212-0912-21111, trace-20250213-1545-90342.

Appendix: quick checklist for oncall or next investigator:
- Pull last 72h traces for route=chat-short, filter p99 > 300ms; group by node and kv-cache-hit flag.
- Plot batch-size vs batch-wait-time scatter; color by node.
- Run synthetic microburst induction against canary with kv-warmup toggled off/on.
- Confirm trace instrumentation coverage and file an observability bug if missing markers.

Owners and contacts:
- Investigation lead: Asha Patel (ashap@redwood.company)
- Batching policy owner: Miguel Ramirez
- KV-cache owner: Lina Chen
- Observability: Evan Goldberg

End of walkthrough.
